---
title: "Testing"
---


Around 200 assertions, all of which run without a Zotero installation and
without network access.

```r
# in the package directory
devtools::test()
# or the full thing
R CMD build . && R CMD check --as-cran qdaR_0.1.0.tar.gz
```

The CRAN check currently reports 0 errors, 0 warnings and 2 notes: the
new-submission note, and one about the local HTML Tidy being too old. Neither
is a property of the package.

## What the suite is actually for

Most of it is ordinary: readers reject malformed files, coefficients match hand
computations, figures build. Two parts are unusual and are the reason the
numbers here can be trusted.

### Congruence with the plugin

`tests/testthat/qdaz-reference.json` holds 109 randomly generated coder
matrices, two to four coders, deliberately skewed marginals, missing ratings —
together with the values the plugin's JavaScript computes for them.
`test-congruence.R` recomputes all six coefficients and compares to twelve
decimal places.

That file is byte-identical to the one in the Python package, and a test there
asserts exactly that. So three implementations in three languages are held to a
single reference rather than to each other.

Agreeing on a hand-picked example proves very little. The fixtures were
generated at random precisely so that no one chose them to make the
implementations agree.

### Congruence with the Python twin on the statistics

`tests/testthat/stats-reference.json` and `stats-fixture.csv` hold 256 codings
over six codes, five documents and two coders, with expected counts small
enough to force the exact-test branch. `test-crosslang.R` pins the chi-squared
statistic, Cramér's V, the Jaccard matrix, the cophenetic correlation, the
scaling distances and the correspondence-analysis inertias.

The two packages compute all of this through entirely different libraries —
`chisq.test`, `cmdscale`, `hclust` and `MASS::corresp` here against scipy and
hand-written linear algebra there, so agreement to twelve decimals is evidence
about the statistics, not about shared code.

Two of these are compared invariantly rather than literally. Scaling
coordinates are only defined up to reflection, so the pairwise distances
between points are compared instead of the coordinates. And the Monte Carlo
p-value is random by construction in both packages, so it is only required to
be close.

**Two real bugs in this package were found this way** and are now pinned by
tests: `qda_chisq()` aborting on a table that was merely awkward, and
`qda_ca()` reporting inertia shares that always summed to 100 %.

### Congruence on the newer measures

Two further frozen references work the same way. `qdaz-e35-reference.json`
covers the unitizing alpha, WindowDiff, Pk, the saturation ratio and the
Wilson interval; `qdaz-gamma-reference.json` covers gamma. Both were computed
by the plugin's JavaScript on randomly generated data and are byte-identical
to the copies in the sibling package, which a test asserts.

Some of these numbers were also checked against the papers themselves rather
than only against each other. The unitizing alpha reproduces the observed
disagreement of 7.8 from Krippendorff's own worked example; the sample-size
functions reproduce Donner and Rotondi's Table 2 in all forty-eight cells and
Fugard and Potts' Table 1 cell for cell; gamma reproduces the three
configurations of Mathet and colleagues' Figure 11, including the negative
value for coders who do worse than chance.

That combination matters. Agreement between three implementations proves they
are consistent; agreement with a published table proves they are right.

## Regenerating a reference

Do this only when a coefficient has legitimately changed on one side, never to
make a failing test pass.

Generate the fixtures once, in whichever language is convenient. Feed them to
the plugin's `src/stats.js` under Node, which takes a `global.QdaZ = {}` and an
`eval` of the file, and to this package. Then compare, and resolve every single
difference before going any further; a reference frozen while two
implementations disagree is worse than no reference. Only then write the new
JSON, into **both** packages, in the same commit.

When picking which fixtures to freeze, make sure the selection covers every
coder count **and** matrices with missing ratings. A regular stride —
`seq(1, n, by = 4)`, once happened to miss every single gap, and the coverage
test in `test-congruence.R` exists to catch exactly that.

## Verifying that a test can fail

A test that has never failed is a claim, not a check. Both congruence tests
were verified by mutation: perturbing the pooled chance term in `qda_fleiss()`
by one part in a million makes the congruence test fail on ten counts. If you
touch these computations, do the same before trusting a green run.

## Non-ASCII

`R/` must contain no non-ASCII characters — CRAN requires it, and it is easy to
introduce accidentally through a copied em-dash or a stray byte-order mark.
`R CMD check` catches it under *checking code files for non-ASCII characters*.
Use `--` and spell out names like Cramer without the accent in code; the
documentation and the vignette may use proper typography.

## Continuous integration

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `R CMD check --as-cran` on Linux, macOS and
Windows, against the current R release and the one before it — the DESCRIPTION
floor is R 4.1. The job fails on a WARNING rather than on a NOTE, because the
two NOTEs in `cran-comments.md` are expected and not defects.

A second job builds the documentation site, so a broken page fails while the
change is still a pull request rather than after the merge.

::: {.callout-warning title="Two tests skip in an ordinary checkout"}

The comparisons that assert a frozen reference is byte-identical to the
copy in qdaPy need the Python package **beside** this one on disk. They
skip in a bare clone, and they skip under `R CMD check` as well, which
copies the tests into a temporary directory where the relative path no
longer resolves.

The `congruence` job therefore checks out both repositories side by side
and runs testthat **in place**, then fails if `sum(df$skipped)` is
anything but zero — a skipped test proves nothing while looking like it
passed. It is switched on by the repository variable `QDAPY_PUBLISHED`
once the Python package has a public repository to check out.
:::
